points: Karl Dietrich Bracher was born on 13 March 1922.
Bracher was born in Stuttgart.
Bracher was German.
Bracher was a political scientist.
Bracher was a historian of the Weimar Republic.
Bracher was a historian of Nazi Germany.
Bracher served in the Wehrmacht during World War II.
American forces captured Bracher while he was serving in Tunisia in 1943.
Bracher was interned at Camp Concordia in Kansas until 1945.
Bracher returned to Germany after his internment.
Bracher studied at the University of Tübingen.
The University of Tübingen awarded Bracher a Ph.D. in classics in 1948.
Bracher studied at Harvard University from 1949 to 1950.
Bracher taught at the Free University of Berlin from 1950 to 1958.
Bracher taught at the University of Bonn from 1959 to 1987.
Bracher became co-publisher of Vierteljahrshefte für Zeitgeschichte, or Quarterly Journal of Contemporary History, in 1978.
Bracher married Dorothee Schleicher in 1951.
Dorothee Schleicher was a niece of Dietrich Bonhoeffer.
Bracher and Dorothee Schleicher had two children.
Bracher died on 19 September 2016.
Bracher was 94 when he died.
Bracher's main concern was how to preserve and develop democracy.
Bracher consistently defended human rights in his work.
Bracher consistently defended pluralism in his work.
Bracher consistently defended constitutional values in his work.
Bracher urged Germans to align themselves with Western democratic values.
Bracher regarded democracy as a fragile institution.
Bracher argued that only a concerned citizenry could safeguard democracy.
Bracher's concern with the fragility of democracy appeared in his first book, Verfall und Fortschritt im Denken der frühen römischen Kaiserzeit, published in 1948.
Bracher's first book examined the downfall of the Roman Republic.
Bracher's first book examined the rise of Augustus.
Bracher published Die Auflösung der Weimarer Republik, or The Disintegration of the Weimar Republic, in 1955.
The Disintegration of the Weimar Republic is Bracher's best-known book.
Bracher attributed the collapse of German democracy to actions resulting from conscious human choices.
Bracher rejected the idea that a special path of German historical development, or Sonderweg, caused the collapse of Weimar democracy.
Bracher rejected explanations that attributed the collapse of Weimar democracy to impersonal forces.
Bracher rejected the Marxist theory that National Socialism resulted from a capitalist conspiracy.
Bracher rejected the theory that the Treaty of Versailles caused the collapse of the Weimar Republic.
Bracher rejected the idea that the Nazi dictatorship was simply the work of fate.
Bracher combined political science and history in The Disintegration of the Weimar Republic.
Bracher's approach to studying Weimar was considered highly innovative in the 1950s.
Bracher's approach to studying Weimar was considered controversial in the 1950s.
The German historian Eberhard Kolb called The Disintegration of the Weimar Republic unsurpassed as research on the republic's end.
Bracher wrote that almost all Germans rejected the Treaty of Versailles.
Bracher denied that opposition to Versailles brought about presidential government in March 1930.
Bracher denied that opposition to Versailles caused the Nazi Party's rise beginning with the September 1930 Reichstag election.
Bracher argued that the judicial system had already become politicized under Weimar.
According to Bracher, almost all Weimar judges had begun their careers in the Imperial era.
Bracher wrote that Weimar judges tended to impose very lenient sentences for political crimes committed in the name of the right.
Bracher held the judiciary partly responsible for Weimar's collapse because it helped authoritarian and totalitarian movements overthrow the republic.
Bracher saw the introduction of presidential government in 1930 as the beginning of the end of the Weimar Republic.
Beginning with Heinrich Brüning's government, chancellors sought to govern without relying on the Reichstag.
Chancellors relied instead on presidential powers under the constitutional articles known as the 25/48/53 formula.
Article 25 allowed the Reich president to dissolve the Reichstag.
Article 48 allowed the Reich president to issue emergency decrees.
Article 53 allowed the Reich president to appoint the chancellor.
The use of the 25/48/53 formula was technically legal.
The use of the 25/48/53 formula violated the spirit of the constitution.
Article 54 made the chancellor and cabinet responsible to the Reichstag.
Bracher argued that the end of German democracy was not inevitable.
Bracher attributed the end of German democracy in part to major errors and failures by Germany's leaders.
Bracher singled out President Paul von Hindenburg for particular responsibility for the end of German democracy.
Bracher divided the collapse of the republic into several stages.
Bracher called the Brüning stage the loss of power.
During the loss-of-power stage, Brüning's cabinet governed solely through Article 48 rather than through the Reichstag.
Bracher called the stage under Franz von Papen and Kurt von Schleicher the power vacuum.
Democracy was gutted during the power-vacuum stage.
Papen failed to build a new system during his short time in office.
Schleicher failed to build a new system during his short time in office.
Bracher identified the National Socialists' seizure of power in 1933 as the final stage of the collapse.
Bracher's terms loss of power and power vacuum referred to the decay of the democratic system rather than a weakening of the state.
Kolb noted that the Reichswehr gained considerable power between 1930 and 1933.
Kolb noted that the bureaucracy gained considerable power between 1930 and 1933.
Kolb noted that the police gained considerable power between 1930 and 1933.
Kolb noted that Hindenburg gained especially dramatic power between 1930 and 1933.
Kolb described German democracy as gradually collapsing between 1930 and 1933.
Kolb noted that the Reichswehr increasingly made policy decisions in place of the Reichstag.
Kolb noted that Hindenburg's inner circle increasingly made policy decisions in place of the Reichstag.
Bracher argued that presidential government was intended to weaken democracy.
Bracher argued that presidential government did weaken democracy.
Bracher argued that no unmanageable parliamentary crisis forced Hindenburg and his chancellors to adopt presidential government.
Bracher maintained that Brüning undermined German democracy.
Bracher maintained that Papen succeeded Brüning and went even further in undermining German democracy.
Bracher's interpretation of Brüning and Papen led to a dispute with Werner Conze.
Conze was a prominent Nazi historian during Nazi rule.
Conze became a leading conservative historian in West Germany in the 1950s.
Conze set out his interpretation of presidential government in a series of articles in the 1950s and 1960s.
Conze argued that German politics had become severely dysfunctional by 1929–1930.
Conze argued that Hindenburg reluctantly introduced presidential government as the only way to keep Germany governable.
Conze regarded Brüning's reliance on Article 48 as temporary.
Conze argued that Brüning used Article 48 to save democracy from the crisis caused by the Great Depression in Germany.
In a series of articles replying to Conze, Bracher documented plans for presidential government dating back at least to 1926.
Bracher argued that Hindenburg sought to do away with democracy well before the Great Depression.
Bracher argued that Hindenburg's inner circle sought to do away with democracy well before the Great Depression.
Bracher argued that the Reichswehr sought to do away with democracy well before the Great Depression.
Bracher said that General Kurt von Schleicher and Brüning had worked out a plan for presidential government by April 1929.
Hindenburg wanted Hermann Müller's government to pass the Young Plan.
The Young Plan referendum of November 1929 delayed passage of the plan.
According to Bracher, Hindenburg's wish to have Müller's government pass the Young Plan kept Müller in office for almost another year.
Bracher saw Brüning's government as the first step toward dismantling democracy rather than an effort to save it.
Brüning's memoirs were published posthumously in 1970.
Brüning's memoirs strongly supported Bracher's interpretation of his government.
Brüning was a conservative Catholic.
Brüning never married.
Brüning is not known to have had a relationship with a woman.
The article portrays Brüning's memoirs as revealing an unhealthy emotional dependence on Hindenburg.
The article portrays Brüning as slavishly devoted to Hindenburg.
The article says Brüning regarded Hindenburg in homoerotic terms as the epitome of German masculinity and strength.
Brüning admitted in his memoirs that presidential government was intended to abolish democracy.
Brüning admitted that presidential government was intended to restore the monarchy by bringing back the exiled Wilhelm II.
Brüning complained that Schleicher had turned Hindenburg against him in the spring of 1932.
Hindenburg dismissed Brüning in May 1932.
Hindenburg replaced Brüning with Papen.
Brüning did not object to Papen's policies in his memoirs.
Brüning said that he would have pursued the same policies as Papen if Hindenburg had given him the chance.
The article says Bracher won the debate with Conze.
As late as 1971, Bracher deplored the tendency to treat presidential government as an attempt to save democracy.
After Brüning's memoirs appeared, Bracher described presidential government as part of a deliberate plan to establish a right-wing regime.
According to Bracher, the planned regime was to operate independently of political parties.
According to Bracher, the planned regime was to operate independently of parliament.
According to Bracher, the plan was meant to keep the Social Democrats out of power.
Bracher argued that Brüning's policies shifted between defending a bureaucratic state based on the rule of law and paving the way for dictatorship.
Bracher rejected the description of Brüning as simply the last chancellor before the breakup of the Weimar Republic.
In a survey of Weimar historiography, Kolb wrote that research since the 1970s had confirmed Bracher's critical assessment of Brüning.
Kolb noted that the evidence for Bracher's assessment of Brüning had been weaker when Bracher first offered it in 1955.
Papen launched the Prussian coup in 1932.
The Prussian coup was also known as the Rape of Prussia.
The Prussian coup removed Otto Braun's Social Democratic government by presidential decree.
Bracher criticized the Social Democrats sharply for failing to resist the Prussian coup.
Bracher believed that the Reichswehr would probably have crushed resistance to the Prussian coup.
Bracher argued that even unsuccessful resistance could have made a lasting show of democratic resolve against a temporarily stronger force.
Bracher argued that such a show of resolve might have saved democratic consciousness from the psychological and moral collapse of republican forces.
Bracher argued that resistance could have made things harder for the new rulers.
Bracher argued that resistance could have delayed later developments.
Bracher argued that resistance could have lessened the effects of later developments.
Bracher described German supporters of democracy as upbeat and determined to take a stand until July 1932.
Bracher said the Prussian coup left supporters of democracy demoralized and passive.
Bracher said supporters of democracy lost their fighting spirit because they felt the rules were rigged against them after the coup.
Bracher's interpretation of the Prussian coup prompted a heated debate with Arnold Brecht.
Brecht argued that there was no way to oppose the coup without breaking the law.
Papen justified the coup by claiming that the Social Democrats and the German Communist Party were about to form a united left.
Papen claimed that the united left would start a Marxist revolution in Germany.
Bracher considered Papen's stated justification for the coup absurd.
Bracher argued that Papen intended to dismantle democracy.
Bracher argued that breaking the law can be justified in defense of democracy.
Bracher regarded Brecht's legal objection to resistance as an excuse for passivity.
Historians have generally agreed with Bracher that breaking the law can be justified in the face of injustice by those in power.
Historians have generally agreed that the Prussian coup was a case in which unlawful resistance in defense of democracy would have been justified.
Bracher held that human choices brought about the National Socialist period.
Bracher traced the roots of National Socialism to nineteenth-century völkisch ideology in Germany and Austria-Hungary.
Bracher believed that this völkisch ideology found its fullest expression in Adolf Hitler's personality.
Bracher thought that too many Germans under Weimar and Nazi rule were willing to give uncritical approval to a strong authoritarian state.
Bracher thought that too many Germans under Weimar and Nazi rule were willing to give quasi-military obedience to a strong authoritarian state.
Although Bracher opposed the Sonderweg as a general interpretation of German history, he believed a distinctive German mentality, or Sonderbewusstsein, helped make Nazi Germany possible.
Bracher argued that the term German Sonderweg should be limited to the Third Reich.
Bracher traced the distinctive German mentality to opposition to the French Revolution.
Bracher argued that the distinctive German mentality grew stronger after 1870.
Bracher argued that the distinctive German mentality grew stronger after 1918.
Bracher argued that the exaggerated ideas and rhetoric of this mentality became a political force.
Bracher argued that what had been a myth became reality.
Bracher argued that the transition from democracy to dictatorship was not unique to Germany.
Bracher linked the radical character of the Nazi dictatorship to the strength of the German ideology that became a totalitarian political reality from 1933 to 1945.
The Sonderbewusstsein Bracher discussed corresponded to the original Sonderweg idea of the Prussian-German state as a unique Central European great power belonging to neither East nor West.
The ideology of Prussian-German uniqueness treated opposition to democracy as part of its opposition to Western civilization.
The 1960 monograph Die nationalsozialistische Machtergreifung, or The National Socialist Seizure of Power, was another well-known work associated with Bracher.
Bracher co-wrote The National Socialist Seizure of Power with Wolfgang Sauer and Gerhard Schulz.
The National Socialist Seizure of Power described in detail how German life was brought into line with the Nazi regime in 1933–1934, a process called Gleichschaltung.
The American historian Walter Laqueur reviewed The National Socialist Seizure of Power.
Laqueur praised Bracher, Sauer, and Schulz for refusing to make excuses for the Nazi regime.
Laqueur praised the authors for asking difficult questions about Germans' conduct under Nazi rule.
Laqueur regretted that works such as William L. Shirer's The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich became bestsellers.
Laqueur considered The National Socialist Seizure of Power far superior to Shirer's book as scholarship.
Laqueur thought The National Socialist Seizure of Power was unlikely ever to be translated into English.
Laqueur thought The National Socialist Seizure of Power was even less likely to become a bestseller.
Bracher regarded Nazi Germany as a totalitarian regime.
Bracher considered Carl Joachim Friedrich and Zbigniew Brzezinski's typology of totalitarianism too rigid.
Bracher argued that models of totalitarianism should be based on careful empirical research.
Bracher argued that Friedrich and Brzezinski overlooked the revolutionary dynamic of totalitarianism.
Bracher regarded the revolutionary dynamic as the core principle of totalitarianism.
Bracher argued that totalitarianism claims the authority to control all aspects of society.
Bracher argued that totalitarianism seeks to remake all aspects of society.
Bracher identified an all-embracing ideology as an essential feature of totalitarianism.
Bracher identified the emphasis on authoritarian leadership as an essential feature of totalitarianism.
Bracher identified the pretense that state and society are one as an essential feature of totalitarianism.
Bracher distinguished a closed totalitarian understanding of politics from an open democratic one.
Bracher defined politics as the struggle for control of state power.
Bracher argued that historians need to supplement traditional historical methods with political science to understand political history properly.
Bracher said that Germans identified enthusiastically with Hitler rather than with Himmler, Bormann, Heydrich, or the Nazi Party itself.
Bracher regarded Germans' identification with Hitler as a central problem for historians, especially German historians.
Bracher argued that German historians should investigate why Germans identified with Hitler without minimizing it.
Bracher argued that ignoring Germans' identification with Hitler would mean abandoning a commitment to historical truth.
Bracher sharply criticized the Marxist view that Nazi leaders were controlled by big business.
Bracher argued for the primacy of politics in Nazi Germany rather than the primacy of economics.
Bracher held that business interests were subordinate to the Nazi dictatorship, like every other part of society.
Bracher argued that Nazi ideology dictated the regime's actions.
Bracher saw the frequent economic irrationality of Nazi actions as evidence for the primacy of politics.
The article associates the functionalist interpretation of Nazi Germany mainly with left-wing historians.
Bracher saw functionalism as an attempt to turn away from the older liberal theory of totalitarianism.
Bracher said functionalists favored a relativizing interpretation that emphasized improvisation in the Nazi exercise of power.
Bracher argued that left-wing interpretations sought to set aside questions of guilt and responsibility in favor of what they considered a more modern, realistic analysis.
Bracher warned that this approach risked underestimating and trivializing National Socialism.
Bracher argued that this approach encouraged vague left-wing talk about fascism and reaction.
In the 1960s, Bracher was a leading critic of Ernst Nolte's theory of generic fascism.
Bracher considered the concept of generic fascism intellectually invalid.
Against Nolte's philosophical idea of the metapolitical, Bracher argued that individual choices by Germans produced National Socialism.
The article calls Bracher's 1969 book Die deutsche Diktatur, or The German Dictatorship, his major work.
Bracher wrote The German Dictatorship partly to rebut Nolte's theory of generic fascism.
The German Dictatorship presented the Nazi regime as a totalitarian dictatorship created by human actions.
The German Dictatorship presented the Nazi regime as a totalitarian dictatorship sustained by human actions.
The German Dictatorship used totalitarianism theory to explain Nazi Germany.
The German Dictatorship used social science methods to explain Nazi Germany.
Bracher advocated treating history as a social science.
As an advocate of history as a social science, Bracher strongly disliked Nolte's philosophical theories of generic fascism.
In a 1971 review, the American historian Lucy Dawidowicz called The German Dictatorship a work of unparalleled distinction.
Dawidowicz praised The German Dictatorship for its scrupulous objectivity.
Dawidowicz praised The German Dictatorship for its passionate commitment to democratic values.
In 1989, the British historian Richard J. Evans called The German Dictatorship valuable.
Bracher often criticized the functionalist-structuralist interpretation of Nazi Germany.
Martin Broszat and Hans Mommsen championed the functionalist-structuralist interpretation.
Bracher rejected the view, associated with Broszat and Mommsen, that Hitler was a weak dictator.
Bracher described Hitler as the master of the Third Reich.

question.text: A country has a democratic constitution, but its citizens pay little attention when leaders undermine democratic institutions. What would Bracher's view suggest about this situation?
options: The constitution is sufficient to safeguard democracy even when citizens remain indifferent.
Democracy remains vulnerable because constitutional rules cannot substitute for an engaged citizenry.
Democracy is best protected by allowing the executive to govern independently of parliament.
Citizens can safeguard democracy simply by deferring to officials who claim to act legally.
